we found that the proportion of undetected celiacs in children with HHLA risk alleles was high.
we have identified a high proportion of celiac disease in young HLA-genotyping children.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the genetic factors that predispose to celiac disease.
the development of new methods for the diagnosis and monitoring of celiac disease and other diseases with autoimmune components, such as diabetes, multiple sclerosis and autoimmune liver disease.
the identification of novel therapeutic strategies for patients with celiac disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a high proportion of children with HLA genotypes DQB1*03 and/or DQB1*05 have celiac disease, which is not diagnosed by the health-care system.
the screening test for celiac disease is positive in 5.1% of the HLA-risk genotyped 3-year-old population and that the proportion of celiac disease is 4.5% in this age group in southern Sweden.
the prevalence of celiac disease in the Swedish population is higher than previously thought.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the prevalence of celiac disease in the general population is much higher than previously assumed.
the prevalence of celiac disease among 3-year old children in Sweden may be as high as 1 in 100.
the screening for tTGAb in HLA-risk children at 3 years is highly efficient in detecting celiac disease, and that the proportion of celiac disease is high among HLA-risk children in Sweden.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a high proportion of undiaggosed celiac disease can be detected by screening in young children at high risk of the disease.
the prevalence of celiac disease in young children with HLA DQ risk is much higher than previously thought.
a large proportion of children with celiac disease remain undiagnosed, even among children with HLA-genotyperisk.
